laws.title: Alcohol Limit — 0.5g/L BAC
laws.subtitle: Greek Traffic Code — Strict holiday enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Greece: 0.5g/L BAC limit. Professional drivers: 0.2g/L. Significantly stricter enforcement during summer tourist season and holidays.
laws.penalty: 0.5–0.8g/L: fine €200–€700 + 3-month suspension. Above 0.8g/L: criminal, up to 2 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Professional and new drivers: 0.2g/L

quiz.q: Greece's BAC limit for general drivers?
quiz.explanation: Greece's general BAC limit is 0.5g/L.

laws.title: Greek Hospitality — Philoxenia (Love of Strangers)
laws.subtitle: Refusing hospitality is deeply offensive
laws.fullDescription: Philoxenia (love of strangers/hospitality) is one of Greece's most important cultural values. Never refuse offered food or drink — to do so is genuinely offensive. Greetings: handshakes (formal) or cheek kisses between friends. Punctuality for social events is flexible. Family and community are central. 'Opa!' is used to express joy and celebration.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — refusing Greek hospitality causes real offence.
exceptions: Business meetings: punctuality is increasingly expected
Athens is more cosmopolitan than rural areas

quiz.q: What is 'philoxenia' in Greek culture?
quiz.explanation: Philoxenia (φιλοξενία) literally means 'love of strangers' and is one of Greece's most important cultural values — hospitality to guests.

laws.title: Open Container and Public Drinking — Local Ordinances
laws.subtitle: Mykonos, Santorini and major tourist islands have restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Greece introduced anti-booze tourism laws targeting popular party islands. Mykonos and Santorini have ordinances restricting public drunkenness, noise after midnight, and in some zones open alcohol containers on the street. The 2023 law also cracked down on party boats ('booze cruises'). Mainland Greece is more relaxed. Disorderly conduct while drunk can lead to immediate detention.
laws.penalty: Public intoxication with disorderly conduct: fine €100–€500. Licensed venue noise violations: fines up to €10,000.
exceptions: Designated outdoor terrace seating at licensed venues
Festival and official event areas

quiz.q: Which Greek islands introduced stricter anti-booze tourism laws in recent years?
quiz.explanation: Mykonos and Santorini introduced ordinances restricting public drinking, noise, and party boats after a crackdown on booze tourism.

laws.title: Antiquities Laws — Taking Historical Artefacts is Serious Crime
laws.subtitle: Law 3028/2002 — Any ancient item removal is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Greece's Cultural Heritage Law (3028/2002) makes it a serious criminal offence to remove, damage, or export any archaeological find — including small items like pottery shards, tiles, or coins from ancient sites. Metal detectors are illegal without permit. Customs authorities actively search bags leaving the country for undeclared antiquities. Even possession can lead to criminal charges.
laws.penalty: Removing antiquities: 10 years minimum imprisonment + heavy fines. Exporting without permit: criminal charges at customs.
exceptions: Licensed archaeologists with official excavation permits
Officially purchased certified reproductions

quiz.q: Is it legal to take a small pottery shard from an ancient Greek site as a souvenir?
options: Yes — if it's on the surface
No — removing any antiquity is a serious criminal offence
Only if you declare it at customs
quiz.explanation: Removing any archaeological artefact in Greece — even a tiny pottery shard — is a criminal offence carrying 10 years minimum imprisonment.

laws.title: Greek Island Beach Rules — Protected Loggerhead Sea Turtles
laws.subtitle: WWF Greece / Presidential Decree — Zakynthos nesting beaches strictly protected
laws.fullDescription: Zakynthos (Zante) hosts one of the Mediterranean's most important loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) nesting beaches at Laganas Bay — a protected National Marine Park. Rules: no beach access at night during nesting season (June–October), no umbrellas/sunbeds in nesting zones, no lighting on the beach at night (disorients hatchlings), no boats in restricted swimming zones. Beach closures are enforced. Violations are a criminal offence under the Marine Park decree. Other Greek islands also have protected zones.
laws.penalty: Beach access during closure: fine €1,000+. Lighting on nesting beach at night: criminal offence. Boat in restricted zone: fine.
exceptions: Licensed research scientists with marine park permit
Park rangers and conservation staff
laws.sourceLabel: Zakynthos National Marine Park — Sea Turtle Protection

quiz.q: Why is nighttime beach access banned at Laganas Bay, Zakynthos during summer?
options: To protect loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) nesting — lights and activity disorient hatchlings
quiz.explanation: Laganas Bay is a critical nesting ground for loggerhead sea turtles — nighttime beach access is banned June–October to protect nesting females and hatchlings, who are fatally disoriented by lights.

laws.title: Archaeological Site Rules — Even a Pebble Can Mean Prison
laws.subtitle: Law 3028/2002 — Removal of any object from an archaeological site is a criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Greece's Law 3028/2002 on the Protection of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage is extraordinarily broad — it criminalises the removal of any object whatsoever from a designated archaeological site or area, including natural stones, fragments of pottery, soil samples, or any item that could conceivably be of archaeological significance. Greece has over 100,000 registered archaeological sites and many unregistered areas of known historical importance, meaning the rules apply across vast swathes of the country. Tourists have been arrested, prosecuted, and convicted for taking what they believed to be ordinary pebbles or rocks from beaches near ancient ruins. Customs and airport security actively check departing travellers' luggage for undeclared items. The law reflects Greece's deep national sensitivity about the loss of its ancient heritage — a sensitivity sharpened by the long-running dispute over the Elgin Marbles removed from the Parthenon in the early 19th century.
laws.penalty: Removing any object from an archaeological site: minimum 2 years imprisonment and fines. Exporting without a permit: 10 years minimum imprisonment. Possession of undeclared antiquities: criminal charges.
exceptions: Licensed archaeologists conducting officially approved excavations with Ministry of Culture permits
Purchasing certified reproductions or modern crafts from licensed shops
laws.sourceLabel: Hellenic Ministry of Culture — Law 3028/2002 on Protection of Antiquities

quiz.q: Under Greek Law 3028/2002, what can happen if you remove an ordinary-looking pebble from an archaeological site?
options: Nothing — small natural objects are exempt
Criminal prosecution with a minimum 2-year prison sentence
A warning on your first offence
quiz.explanation: Greek law makes it a criminal offence to remove any object from an archaeological site, regardless of how trivial it appears. Tourists have been prosecuted and imprisoned for taking pebbles or small stones from areas near ancient ruins — minimum sentences start at 2 years.

laws.title: Mount Athos — ‘Avaton’ Rule Forbids Women on the Monastic Peninsula
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Charter of Mount Athos 1924 — Men only; Diamonitirion permit required
laws.fullDescription: Mount Athos, the autonomous monastic republic on the Chalkidiki peninsula, has enforced an ‘avaton’ (no-entry rule for females) for over 1,000 years. The prohibition applies to women and to female domestic animals (a small number of cats and laying hens are exempt). The Constitutional Charter of Mount Athos of 1924, recognised in Article 105 of the Greek Constitution, gives the peninsula legal autonomy and protects the avaton tradition. Male visitors of any faith may apply for a Diamonitirion (entry permit) through the Pilgrim’s Office in Thessaloniki; about 100 Orthodox Christian and 10 non-Orthodox permits are issued per day. The European Parliament has called for repeal; Greek government and Mount Athos authorities have consistently refused on grounds of religious freedom and tradition. Female visitors can view the monasteries by sea from an exclusion distance of 500 m enforced by the Greek Coast Guard. Several women who attempted entry over the decades have been arrested and tried. In 2008 four Moldovan women who were trafficked onto Athos by mistake were immediately removed.
laws.penalty: Woman entering Mount Athos: up to 12 months imprisonment under Article 3 of the Monastic Regulation Decree 2623/1953. Male visitor entering without Diamonitirion: detention and expulsion.
exceptions: No exceptions for women — the avaton is absolute
Male visitors with a valid Diamonitirion issued by the Pilgrim’s Office
laws.sourceLabel: Constitutional Charter of Mount Athos 1924 / Article 105 Greek Constitution

quiz.q: What is the legal status of women visiting Mount Athos in Greece?
options: Permitted if escorted by a male monk
Prohibited — ‘avaton’ rule, up to 12 months imprisonment
quiz.explanation: Mount Athos’s 1,000-year ‘avaton’ bans women from the peninsula. Violation can result in up to 12 months imprisonment under Monastic Regulation Decree 2623/1953, backed by Article 105 of the Greek Constitution.

laws.title: Loggerhead Sea Turtle Protection — Zakynthos Nesting Beaches Strictly Regulated
laws.subtitle: Presidential Decree 906/1981 — Caretta caretta nesting areas: no development, no lights
laws.fullDescription: The loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) nests on several Greek beaches — Zakynthos (Zante) hosts the largest nesting population in the Mediterranean at Laganas Bay, which is a Marine National Park. Greek law strictly prohibits: beach umbrellas or sunbeds in nesting zones, night-time lighting near nesting beaches (artificial lights disorient hatchlings), music and noise on nesting beaches after sunset, and boat racing in protected waters. Disturbing a nesting female or her eggs is a criminal offence. From May to October (nesting season), beach access in core zones is restricted after sunset. The Archelon Sea Turtle Protection Society monitors nesting and works with authorities.
laws.penalty: Disturbing a nesting turtle or eggs: up to 2 years imprisonment + €30,000 fine. Operating sunbeds in a protected nesting zone: administrative fine + removal order.
exceptions: Archelon researchers and licensed marine biologists with Ministry of Environment permit
Emergency lighting for vessel safety in port approaches
laws.sourceLabel: Archelon Sea Turtle Protection Society — Greece

quiz.q: Where is the largest loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) nesting site in the Mediterranean?
quiz.explanation: Laganas Bay on Zakynthos (Zante) island hosts the largest Caretta caretta nesting population in the Mediterranean — protected as a Marine National Park with strict regulations on beach activities during the May–October nesting season.

laws.title: Fire Season Restrictions — Greece's Strict Wildfire Prevention Laws
laws.subtitle: Summer fire bans are comprehensive; violations during red-alert days carry prison sentences
laws.fullDescription: Following catastrophic wildfires (2007 Peloponnese, 2018 Mati, 2023 Evros), Greece enacted some of Europe's strictest wildfire prevention laws. The 'fire season' officially runs May 1 – October 31. During this period: open fires, BBQs, burning of agricultural waste, and smoking outdoors in forested areas are prohibited. On 'high-risk' (Category 3) days, no activity that could cause sparks is permitted within 10 meters of forest. On 'extreme-risk' (Category 5) days, access to many forests is completely banned. Agricultural burning requires advance permits and can only occur in specific months. Electrical equipment in forests must be inspected and certified.
laws.penalty: Arson causing wildfire: 10 years–life imprisonment. Negligent fire-starting: 3–10 years. Illegal burning during prohibited period: fines €3,000–€30,000 + criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Controlled burns by licensed professionals with prefect permits
Traditional village festivals with certified safety measures
Emergency heating in power outage situations
laws.sourceLabel: Greek Civil Protection — Fire Season Regulations

quiz.q: When is Greece's official 'fire season' during which outdoor burning is broadly prohibited?
quiz.explanation: Greece's official fire season runs May 1 to October 31, during which open fires, agricultural burning, and smoking in forested areas are broadly prohibited to prevent the catastrophic wildfires that have repeatedly devastated the country.

laws.title: Elgin Marbles (Parthenon Sculptures) — Greece's Ongoing Repatriation Legal Demand
laws.subtitle: Greece has formally demanded return of British Museum Parthenon sculptures since 1983
laws.fullDescription: The Parthenon sculptures removed by Lord Elgin between 1801–1812 (approximately 50% of surviving ancient sculptures from the Acropolis) are housed in the British Museum, which refuses to return them citing the British Museum Act 1963 (which prohibits permanent deaccessioning). Greece's Melina Mercouri Foundation and successive governments have formally requested repatriation since 1983. Greece built the Acropolis Museum (2009) specifically to house reunified sculptures — it has empty display spaces waiting for the marbles to return. In 2023, UK PM Rishi Sunak canceled a meeting with Greek PM Kyriakos Mitsotakis over the issue. The same year, the Vatican returned a fragment it held to Greece. Many international polls show majority support for return. UNESCO has called for negotiated resolution.
laws.penalty: The dispute is a diplomatic and legal matter between states — not a domestic criminal law issue. Within Greece, unauthorized excavation or removal of archaeological artifacts: up to 10 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Existing agreements for temporary loans of Greek artifacts to foreign museums
Bilateral cultural exchange treaties for non-Acropolis artifacts
Greek nationals may view the Elgin Marbles in the British Museum freely
laws.sourceLabel: Acropolis Museum — Parthenon Sculptures Return Campaign

quiz.q: Why can the British Museum legally refuse to return the Parthenon Sculptures to Greece?
options: International law permits indefinite retention of wartime acquisitions
The British Museum Act 1963 prohibits permanent deaccessioning of its collection
Greece signed an agreement in 1832 waiving repatriation rights
UN cultural property treaties exempt items acquired before 1954
quiz.explanation: The British Museum Act 1963 prohibits the museum from permanently deaccessioning items from its collection — meaning even if museum trustees wanted to return the Parthenon Sculptures, they would need UK Parliamentary legislation to do so. Greece argues the sculptures were removed under duress and their original removal was illegal.

laws.title: Greek Migration Management — Lesbos, Moria Fire, and EU Asylum Law Tensions
laws.subtitle: Greece is EU's migration frontline; Moria camp fire 2020 exposed systemic failures in asylum law
laws.fullDescription: Greece manages one of Europe's highest levels of first asylum applications due to its position on the Aegean Sea migration route. The Moria refugee camp on Lesbos housed 13,000+ people in a facility designed for 3,000 — a product of the EU-Turkey Statement (2016) keeping migrants on Greek islands. In September 2020, Moria burned to the ground in a fire, leaving 12,000 people homeless. Greek authorities faced criticism for pushback practices in the Aegean — Turkish coast guard and NGOs documented incidents. Greece's asylum law has been amended multiple times to comply with EU law while managing large numbers. The EU Migration Pact (2024) distributes asylum seekers among EU member states — Greece lobbied for this for years. Frontex (EU border agency) has been deployed to Greek waters.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized border crossing: detention pending asylum processing. Failed asylum seekers: deportation orders. Smuggling migrants: up to 10 years imprisonment. Greek coast guard pushbacks: subject to EU investigation.
exceptions: UNHCR-registered refugees have status protection during appeals
Unaccompanied minors have enhanced procedural rights under EU law
EU citizens have free movement rights regardless of migration rules

quiz.q: What 2016 agreement kept asylum seekers on Greek islands, leading to massively overcrowded conditions including the Moria camp crisis?
quiz.explanation: The EU-Turkey Statement (March 2016) required asylum seekers arriving in Greece to remain on the Greek islands while their applications were processed — rather than traveling to the mainland. This created severely overcrowded conditions on Lesbos, Samos, and other islands, with Moria camp housing 13,000+ people in facilities designed for 3,000.

laws.title: Tempi Train Disaster & Railway Negligence
laws.subtitle: Greece's deadliest peacetime rail accident (57 dead) exposed criminal negligence in railway safety
laws.fullDescription: On February 28, 2023, two passenger trains collided head-on near Larissa in the Tempi valley — Greece's deadliest peacetime railway accident, killing 57 people, mostly university students returning from Carnival. Investigation revealed systemic criminal negligence: Larissa's stationmaster manually authorized both trains on the same track because the safety signaling system had been non-functional for years, no ATP (automatic train protection) system existed, and railway management had failed to address repeated safety warnings. Nationwide strikes followed. The stationmaster was convicted; senior railway officials face manslaughter charges. Greece accelerated railway safety modernization with EU funds.
laws.penalty: Stationmaster convicted of manslaughter: 10 years imprisonment. Railway management officials: facing charges for criminal negligence. OSE (Hellenic Railways) officials: civil and criminal liability for systemic safety failures.
exceptions: EU railway safety directives require ATP systems — Greece had been non-compliant for years
Families received compensation from both OSE and state
Survivors' testimony was central evidence in criminal proceedings
laws.sourceLabel: Greek Ministry of Infrastructure — Tempi Investigation

quiz.q: How many people died in Greece's 2023 Tempi train collision?
quiz.explanation: The February 2023 Tempi train collision killed 57 people — mostly university students — in Greece's deadliest peacetime railway accident. The disaster revealed that safety signaling systems had been non-functional for years due to criminal negligence.

laws.title: Golden Visa Reform & Housing Crisis
laws.subtitle: Greece raised its Golden Visa threshold to €800,000 in major cities as housing costs surged
laws.fullDescription: Greece's Golden Visa program, launched in 2013 during the financial crisis, offered EU residency for €250,000 property investment — the EU's lowest threshold. It became hugely popular: over 12,000 visas issued, generating €4+ billion. However, Athens and Thessaloniki experienced severe housing shortages as foreign investors outbid residents. In May 2024, the threshold was raised to €800,000 for Athens, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, and Santorini — and €400,000 for the rest of Greece. Critics argued it was too little too late; rents in central Athens doubled in five years. Short-term rental (Airbnb) regulations were also tightened, requiring registration and limiting new licenses in popular areas.
laws.penalty: Operating a short-term rental without registration: fines up to €50,000. Golden Visa fraud: criminal prosecution and deportation. Property acquired through Golden Visa cannot be sold for 5 years without losing residency.
exceptions: Conversion of commercial properties to residential housing has simplified permits
Restoration of listed buildings maintains the lower €250,000 threshold in all regions
Golden Visa holders can renew every 5 years indefinitely without continuous residence

quiz.q: What is the Golden Visa investment threshold in Athens as of May 2024?
quiz.explanation: Greece raised the Golden Visa threshold to €800,000 for Athens, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, and Santorini in May 2024, up from the original €250,000 that had been the EU's lowest minimum — responding to a housing crisis where central Athens rents doubled in five years.

laws.title: Greek Debt Crisis: Austerity Laws & the Referendum That Was Overruled
laws.subtitle: Greece voted 61% against EU austerity in a 2015 referendum — then accepted even harsher terms days later under threat of Euro exit
laws.fullDescription: Greece's sovereign debt crisis (2009–2018) required three EU/IMF bailouts totaling €289 billion. In July 2015, PM Tsipras called a referendum on EU creditor demands, which Greeks rejected by 61.3%. Days later, Tsipras accepted terms even harsher than those rejected — including pension cuts, tax hikes, privatizations, and loss of fiscal sovereignty to EU creditor supervision. The episode was widely seen as demonstrating the limits of democratic sovereignty within the eurozone. Greece's primary surplus requirements under its bailout program persisted through 2022. Youth unemployment peaked at 60% in 2013. Over 500,000 skilled Greeks emigrated in the 'brain drain' decade.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion (historically pervasive): increased penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment under austerity-era reforms. Capital controls (2015): limits of €60/day ATM withdrawals enforced by banking regulations
exceptions: Pensioners over 70 and those with health conditions received higher ATM withdrawal limits during capital controls
Some privatization requirements were later renegotiated under the third bailout program

quiz.q: By what margin did Greeks vote against EU austerity measures in the July 2015 referendum?
quiz.explanation: Greek voters rejected EU creditor demands by 61.3% in the July 5, 2015 referendum — but PM Tsipras then accepted even harsher terms days later under threat of being forced out of the eurozone, overriding the democratic result.

laws.title: Predatorgate: Greece's Spyware Scandal & Mass Politician Wiretapping
laws.subtitle: Greece's intelligence service was found to have wiretapped the opposition leader, journalists, and EU officials using Predator spyware — triggering a constitutional crisis
laws.fullDescription: In 2022, Greece's 'Predatorgate' scandal revealed that the National Intelligence Service (EYP) had wiretapped opposition leader Nikos Androulakis (also an MEP) using state wiretapping combined with Predator commercial spyware. Journalist Thanasis Koukakis and dozens of others were also targeted. The Greek government admitted the EYP surveillance but claimed it was legal under national security provisions; it denied knowledge of the Predator spyware component. The European Parliament's PEGA Committee found Greece in violation of EU privacy law. PM Mitsotakis's nephew — who ran the PM's digital office — resigned. The scandal was one of the most serious EU spyware abuses revealed by the Pegasus/Predator investigation.
laws.penalty: Illegal wiretapping: up to 10 years imprisonment and unlimited fines under Greek law. The government argued the EYP wiretapping was legal under national security exceptions
exceptions: National security wiretapping has reduced judicial oversight in Greece compared to most EU states
The PEGA Committee's findings are advisory — they cannot compel domestic prosecution

quiz.q: Who was the most high-profile target of Greece's 'Predatorgate' wiretapping scandal?
options: Opposition leader Nikos Androulakis, also a member of the European Parliament
quiz.explanation: Opposition leader Nikos Androulakis — also a Member of the European Parliament — was wiretapped by both the Greek intelligence service and Predator commercial spyware. His MEP status made the wiretapping a direct EU-level scandal, triggering the European Parliament's PEGA investigation.

laws.title: Antiquities Ownership Law
laws.subtitle: All ancient artifacts found in Greece belong to the state
laws.fullDescription: Greece's Law 3028/2002 on the Protection of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage declares that all objects dating from prehistoric through Byzantine periods (up to 1453 AD), and modern objects of cultural significance, are the inalienable property of the Greek state. Any antiquity discovered — even on private land — automatically belongs to the state. Unauthorized excavation, possession, trade, or export of antiquities is a serious criminal offense. Greece is one of the most aggressive countries in pursuing the return of cultural property from foreign museums, most famously demanding the return of the Parthenon Marbles (Elgin Marbles) from the British Museum.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment for unauthorized excavation; confiscation of objects; fines up to €1 million
exceptions: Authorized archaeological excavations under academic or state supervision are permitted
Objects documented as being outside Greece before 1970 may be legally held abroad under UNESCO convention

quiz.q: What are the 'Elgin Marbles' and where are they currently held?
options: Parthenon sculptures held in the British Museum
quiz.explanation: The Elgin Marbles (Parthenon Marbles) are sculptures from the Parthenon in Athens, removed by Lord Elgin in the early 1800s and now held at the British Museum. Greece has been demanding their return for decades.

laws.title: Island Property Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Greece restricts foreign ownership of property in border islands for national security
laws.fullDescription: Greece's Law 1892/1990 and subsequent regulations restrict property purchases by non-EU citizens in 'sensitive border areas' — including many Aegean islands close to Turkey, as well as northern border regions. Non-EU foreigners must obtain special permission from the Ministry of Defence, which is rarely granted for areas deemed strategically sensitive. This has been partly relaxed for EU citizens post-EU membership, but Greek-Turkish tensions mean Aegean island restrictions remain strict. Greece also has 'Golden Visa' provisions allowing non-EU citizens to obtain residency through property investment in non-restricted areas (minimum €500,000 investment in certain zones as of 2023).
laws.penalty: Unauthorized purchase of restricted property: sale invalidated; fines; potential criminal charges for facilitating illegal transactions
exceptions: EU citizens are not subject to the same restrictions
Investment property through the Golden Visa scheme is permitted in non-sensitive areas
laws.sourceLabel: Greek Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport

quiz.q: Why does Greece restrict non-EU property purchases in certain Aegean islands?
options: For national security reasons related to proximity to Turkey
To limit population growth in fragile ecosystems
quiz.explanation: Greece restricts non-EU property purchases in many Aegean islands for national security reasons — the islands' proximity to Turkey and ongoing Greek-Turkish territorial disputes make unrestricted foreign property ownership strategically sensitive.

laws.title: Memorandum of Understanding Austerity
laws.subtitle: Greece's bailout agreements required sweeping legal and economic reforms
laws.fullDescription: Greece signed three 'Memoranda of Understanding' (MoU) with the European Commission, ECB, and IMF (the 'Troika') in 2010, 2012, and 2015, receiving €289 billion in bailout loans. In exchange, Greece enacted sweeping austerity laws: pension cuts (averaging 40% reduction), wage cuts (civil servants lost up to 25%), VAT increases, privatization of state assets (airports, ports, utilities), and labor market deregulation. The austerity sparked massive protests (2010–2015) and the rise of Syriza (radical left) and Golden Dawn (neo-Nazi) parties. GDP fell 26% over 2008–2013. Greece exited its final bailout program in August 2018 but still faces primary surplus requirements until 2060.
laws.penalty: Greece's breach of MoU commitments would trigger suspension of loan disbursements; individual violations of austerity laws carry administrative and criminal penalties
exceptions: Humanitarian minimum provisions were maintained even during deepest austerity — no complete welfare cutoffs

quiz.q: By how much did Greece's GDP fall between 2008 and 2013?
quiz.explanation: Greece's GDP fell approximately 26% between 2008 and 2013 — one of the deepest and most prolonged economic contractions experienced by a developed country in peacetime, comparable to the US Great Depression.

laws.title: Same-Sex Marriage Legalization (2024)
laws.subtitle: Greece became the first Orthodox-majority country to legalize same-sex marriage
laws.fullDescription: On February 15, 2024, Greece's parliament voted 176-76 to legalize same-sex marriage, making Greece the first country with a majority Eastern Orthodox Christian population to do so. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis of the conservative New Democracy party supported the bill — a notable move given the party's traditional values base. The law grants same-sex couples identical legal rights to heterosexual couples including marriage, adoption rights, inheritance, and hospital visitation. The Greek Orthodox Church strongly opposed the bill, with the Archbishop of Athens calling it a 'social and moral anomaly.' The vote marked a significant shift in Greek social conservatism, driven by generational change and LGBTQ+ rights advocacy. Greece had previously enacted civil partnerships (2015, extended to same-sex couples only after EU pressure) and registered partnerships for same-sex couples.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against same-sex married couples in employment, housing, or services: civil and administrative penalties; marriage officiants must perform legal marriages regardless of personal beliefs
exceptions: Religious ceremonies remain at the discretion of religious institutions
The Greek Orthodox Church is not required to perform same-sex marriages
Adoption may have additional procedural requirements compared to heterosexual couples initially

laws.title: Troika Memorandums and Austerity Legacy
laws.subtitle: Greece's three bailout programs (2010-2018) required sweeping legal changes as conditionality
laws.fullDescription: Greece received three international bailout programs totaling approximately €289 billion from the EU, ECB, and IMF ('Troika') between 2010 and 2018 in response to its fiscal and debt crisis. Each program required Greece to enact extensive legal changes as conditionality: labor law reforms reducing minimum wages, collective bargaining rights, and dismissal protections; pension cuts (repeated rounds reducing pensions by 40%+ cumulatively); privatization of state assets; tax system reform; healthcare cuts; and changes to product market regulations. These were enacted through 'Memorandums' which legally bound Greece to specific policy actions. The Syriza government elected in January 2015 attempted to renegotiate the memorandum terms and held a referendum (July 2015, 61% voted 'No' to bailout conditions), but ultimately accepted a third bailout with even stricter conditions. Greece exited the last bailout in August 2018 but remained under enhanced surveillance. Recovery has been slow; the constitutional obligation to achieve primary surpluses persists in revised form.
laws.penalty: Greece's failure to meet memorandum targets triggered disbursement holds; domestic implementation of required laws was enforced through troika review missions; legal challenges to austerity laws were largely rejected by Greek courts
exceptions: Greece's constitution's socio-economic rights provisions created constitutional challenges to some cuts
Pensioners below a dignity threshold had partial protection from the deepest cuts
EU fundamental rights framework limited some labor flexibility measures

laws.title: Predatorgate – Illegal Surveillance of Politicians and Journalists
laws.subtitle: Greece faced Europe's worst spyware scandal with government officials wiretapped
laws.fullDescription: The 'Predatorgate' scandal revealed that Greek intelligence services (EYP) and private actors used Predator spyware — similar to Pegasus — to surveil journalists, opposition politicians, and EU officials. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis initially admitted authorizing surveillance of opposition leader Nikos Androulakis (also an MEP) under 'national security' justification before later denying knowledge. The EU Parliament investigated. Greece's National Transparency Authority found multiple illegal wiretapping operations. The scandal led to electoral setbacks for New Democracy in the June 2023 European Parliament elections. Greece has some of Europe's weakest whistleblower and press freedom protections, consistently ranking near the bottom of EU press freedom indices.
laws.penalty: Illegal wiretapping under Law 2225/1994: up to 10 years imprisonment. Unauthorized use of surveillance tools by state actors: criminal prosecution and civil damages.
exceptions: EYP (intelligence service) may surveil under court authorization for national security
Surveillance of communications requires judicial warrant except in narrow national security contexts

quiz.q: Who was among those confirmed to have been surveilled in Greece's Predatorgate scandal?
options: Opposition leader and MEP Nikos Androulakis
quiz.explanation: PM Mitsotakis admitted that intelligence services had surveilled Nikos Androulakis — leader of the PASOK opposition and a Member of the European Parliament — using legal wiretapping under national security justification, but the broader use of Predator spyware proved far wider.

laws.title: Greek Wildfires and Emergency Climate Adaptation Legislation
laws.subtitle: Greece enacted new firefighting and forest protection laws after record-breaking fires
laws.fullDescription: Greece experienced devastating wildfires in 2021 (Evia), 2023 (Evros — largest EU wildfire ever recorded at 96,000 hectares), and 2024 (Attica near Athens). The scale and frequency prompted major legal reforms. Greece passed legislation allowing rebuilding in burned areas (previously prohibited to discourage arson for development), created new aerial firefighting capacity requirements, and established a new Forest Register to prevent illegal development. The 2023 Evros fire killed 18 migrants in a border zone amid allegations of delayed response. Greece also faced EU fines for inadequate nature protection. Climate change has extended the fire season and intensified drought conditions across the Mediterranean.
laws.penalty: Arson causing environmental damage: up to 15 years imprisonment. Illegal construction in burned forest: demolition and fines up to €200,000. Negligent fire-starting: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Traditional agricultural burning with permit during specified periods permitted
Prescribed burns by Forestry Service for fire prevention permitted

quiz.q: What record did Greece's 2023 Evros wildfire set?
options: The deadliest wildfire in Greek history
The largest wildfire ever recorded in the European Union at 96,000 hectares
The first wildfire to reach Athens
The longest duration wildfire in European history
quiz.explanation: The 2023 Evros wildfire burned approximately 96,000 hectares — becoming the largest wildfire ever recorded in the European Union's history, exceeding even the devastating 2021 Evia fires.

laws.title: Greek Migration and Asylum Law Reforms
laws.subtitle: Greece's controversial pushback policies and border management
laws.fullDescription: Greece has faced significant controversy and legal challenges over its migration policies, particularly alleged pushbacks of migrants at sea and land borders, which human rights organizations say violate EU and international law. The 2020 asylum reform law reduced processing times and increased border detention capacity. Greece operates hotspot facilities on Aegean islands (Lesbos, Chios, Samos) under EU funding. The EU-Turkey Statement of 2016, which Greece implements, returns irregular migrants to Turkey if deemed safe third country.
laws.penalty: Irregular entry into Greece: detention up to 18 months pending asylum processing or deportation. Smuggling migrants: 10 years imprisonment minimum, up to life if deaths occur. Human trafficking: up to 20 years imprisonment
exceptions: Recognized refugees receive 3-year residence permits
Unaccompanied minors have special protection procedures
